name: Nick Leeson

summary.text: Nicholas Leeson was the general manager of Baring Futures (Singapore), the SIMEX futures subsidiary of Barings, and controlled both its trading and its settlements. He concealed unauthorised trading losses in an error account numbered 88888 opened in July 1992; the losses brought down the Barings group in February 1995. The Bank of England's Board of Banking Supervision reported in July 1995 that the losses arose from unauthorised and concealed trading within Baring Futures Singapore and that Barings' management and controls had failed. Singapore-appointed inspectors made similar findings. On 1 December 1995 Leeson pleaded guilty in Singapore to two fraud and forgery charges and was sentenced to six and a half years in prison.

facts.claim: On 3 July 1992 Leeson opened an error account, numbered 88888, for Baring Futures Singapore; by the end of September 1992 the losses in it had reached S$8.8 million.
facts.quote: On 3 July, Leeson opened an error account, 88888, for BFS. Its losses were S$8.8 million by the end of September 1992.

facts.claim: Account 88888 was originally opened to record error trades by inexperienced staff; Leeson used it for his unauthorised trading. An internal audit in 1994 reported the risk of Leeson controlling both dealing and settlement, but the bank kept him in both roles because of his experience and the profits he had generated.
facts.quote: An internal audit in 1994 reported the risks of Leeson controlling both dealing and settlement, but the bank kept him in place because of his experience and the profits he had generated.

facts.claim: The Board of Banking Supervision's report of July 1995 concluded that the losses were incurred by reason of unauthorised and concealed trading activities within Baring Futures Singapore, that the true position was not noticed because of a failure of controls and management confusion within Barings, and that the problem was not identified by external auditors, supervisors or regulators before the collapse.
facts.quote: the losses were incurred by reason of unauthorised and concealed trading activities within BFS

sources.title: Implications of the Barings Collapse for Bank Supervisors

facts.claim: The Board of Banking Supervision found that the unusually high profits reported from Singapore in 1994 should have been viewed as abnormal and questionable by Barings management, and that those with direct executive responsibility for establishing effective controls must bear much of the blame.
facts.quote: those profits should have been viewed as abnormal and questionable

sources.title: Implications of the Barings Collapse for Bank Supervisors

facts.claim: The Reserve Bank of Australia's summary of the British inquiry describes a virtual total failure of risk management systems and controls at Barings, together with managerial confusion, weak separation of duties, failure to question extraordinary profits and slow action on internal audit warnings.
facts.quote: virtual total failure of risk management systems and controls

sources.title: Implications of the Barings Collapse for Bank Supervisors

facts.claim: Inspectors appointed by the Singapore government, whose work was carried out by Price Waterhouse, attributed the collapse of Baring Futures Singapore partly to institutional incompetence, found that Barings chief executive Peter Norris had tried to conceal and play down Leeson's unauthorised dealing, and said key individuals in the Baring group's management may have been grossly negligent or wilfully blind.
facts.quote: key individuals of the Baring Group's management may have been grossly negligent or wilfully blind

facts.claim: On 1 December 1995 Leeson pleaded guilty in Singapore to two charges of fraud and forgery and was sentenced to six and a half years in prison; nine other counts were taken into consideration. He was released in July 1999.
facts.quote: He pleaded guilty to two charges of fraud and forgery on 1 December, and was sentenced to six and a half years in prison in Singapore.

sources.title: December 2, 1995: Whiz-kid trader Nick Leeson jailed

connections.claim: Leeson ran Baring Futures (Singapore), the Barings group's SIMEX futures subsidiary, controlling both its trading and its settlements; his concealed losses in account 88888 caused the group's collapse in February 1995.
connections.quote: the losses were incurred by reason of unauthorised and concealed trading activities within BFS

connections.claim: Singapore's inspectors reported that Barings chief executive Peter Norris tried to conceal Leeson's unauthorised dealing and played down its significance, assisted by James Bax and Anthony Hawes.
connections.quote: The report said Barings chief executive Peter Norris tried to conceal Leeson's unauthorised dealing and had played down its significance.

openQuestions: The site says account 88888 hid 'over 60,000' unhedged Nikkei futures contracts; no returned source gave a contract count. Loss figures returned differ by date and currency (S$373.9 million at end-1994; over 827 million pounds by 27 February 1995 in one secondary source).

The site's claim that Leeson booked a fictitious receivable against Spear, Leeds & Kellogg (SLK) was not found in the sources returned; it is in the Board of Banking Supervision report, which should be opened directly.
The site says ING bought Barings for 1 pound; this was not among the results returned.

The Board of Banking Supervision report itself (July 1995) was not retrieved; its findings are cited here through the Chancellor's Hansard statement and the RBA summary. A blog quotes the report as saying no one in management accepted responsibility for Leeson's activities between October 1993 and 1 January 1995; verify against the report.
The Singapore inspectors' findings are cited through a Reuters archive record; the inspectors' report itself (Ministry of Finance, 1995) was not retrieved.
The site's description of Ron Baker as head of the Financial Products Group was not examined.
